lead: A region is a blob of pixels that belong together. A few numbers can describe it instead of a pixel list. Area and perimeter give size and roundness. Topology counts pieces and holes. Texture describes how grey levels are arranged inside. Vision programs use these numbers: a PCB inspector checks pad holes, a rice grader checks grain area and elongation, a fabric grader checks co-occurrence contrast, a cell counter checks nucleus roundness.
prereq: You need: 4.5 and 4.4 for getting the regions themselves, and 4.8 for the boundary numbers these descriptors build on.

blocks.text: Once thresholding or region growing gives a set of pixels, pass a few numbers, not the pixel list.
Area A is the pixel count, in pixels². Perimeter P is boundary length: count boundary pixels, or use chain-code length with √2 for each diagonal step.

blocks.where: P is perimeter in pixels, A is area in pixels², and the result is dimensionless. A circle of radius r has P = 2πr and A = πr², so P²/A = 4π ≈ 12.57. Every other shape scores higher; a long thin streak scores in the hundreds.

blocks.text: Eccentricity uses second moments about the centroid (x̄, ȳ). These mix coordinates, so they capture orientation as well as spread.

blocks.where: the sum runs over region pixels; μ20 and μ02 measure spread along x and y, μ11 measures tilt. The principal axis angle is θ = ½ atan2(2μ11, μ20 − μ02).

blocks.text: Along the principal axes the spreads are a and b, with a ≥ b. Eccentricity is e = √(1 − b²/a²): e = 0 for a disk, close to 1 for a rod.
Grey-level mean inside the region is m = (1/A) Σ f(x, y) and variance is σ² = (1/A) Σ (f(x, y) − m)², both summed over region pixels.
The skeleton, or medial axis, is the set of points with two nearest boundary points. It is one pixel wide, keeps topology, and is used for handwriting or blood-vessel tracing.
Topology ignores size and shape. Only two counts matter.

items: C = number of connected components of the object.
H = number of holes, that is, background components fully enclosed by the object.
The Euler number is E = C − H.

blocks.text: Use 8-connectivity for the object and 4-connectivity for the background, or the reverse. Never the same rule for both. With 8 for both, a diagonal object chain and the diagonal background chain between them would each count as connected, and a closed loop would fail to separate inside from outside. One rule per side keeps C and H consistent, so E comes out the same either way.

E is the cheapest defect test in industry: a machined pad should have exactly one hole, so any change in E flags a broken or blocked hole. C counts rice grains on a conveyor or cells on a slide. These counts survive stretching, rotation and scaling.

sections.h3: Texture: how the grey levels are arranged

blocks.text: Texture is the pattern of grey levels inside the region, not a single pixel value. Sand and knitted cloth can share a mean grey of 128 and still look different.
First-order measures use only the histogram. Normalise it: p_i = n_i / N, the fraction of region pixels at level i, with N the pixel count.

items: Mean: m = Σ i p_i, in grey levels.
Smoothness: R = 1 − 1/(1 + σ²), which is 0 for a flat region and tends to 1 as spread grows.

Third moment: Σ (i − m)³ p_i, the skewness; negative means the histogram is skewed to the left: a long tail toward dark levels while most pixels are bright; positive means a tail toward bright levels.
Uniformity: U = Σ p_i², which is 1 when a single level dominates.
Entropy: H_e = −Σ p_i log₂ p_i, in bits; 0 for a flat region, maximal at log₂ L for L levels used equally.

blocks.text: Uniformity and entropy always move in opposite directions: one dominant level means high U and low H_e.

Second-order measures keep position. The grey-level co-occurrence matrix P(i, j | d, θ) holds the fraction of pixel pairs where one pixel has level i and the pixel at distance d and angle θ has level j; θ is 0°, 45°, 90° or 135°.

items: Contrast: Σ (i − j)² P(i, j) — large when neighbouring levels differ a lot.
Correlation: how linearly aligned i and j are; 1 for a perfect linear relation.
Energy: Σ P(i, j)² — high when the matrix is concentrated in a few cells.
Homogeneity: Σ P(i, j) / (1 + |i − j|) — high when pairs differ by little.

figure.caption: The ring of 1s in the top left encloses one background pixel at row 1, column 1: one hole. The other two groups of 1s are separate components with no holes.

spec.title: Counting components and holes
spec.aria: A 5 by 5 binary image with three separate groups of 1s, one of which surrounds a single 0 hole.

examples.question: Question (a): for the 5×5 binary image in the figure, find C, H and the Euler number using 8-connectivity for the object and 4-connectivity for the background. Question (b): a region has grey-level probabilities 0.50, 0.25, 0.15 and 0.10 at levels 0, 1, 2 and 3. Find the mean, the second moment, the variance, the uniformity and the entropy.
steps: Label the 1s with 8-connectivity: the ring in rows 0–2, columns 0–2 is one component.
(1,4) and (2,4) are the second component; (4,0) and (4,1) are the third. So C = 3.
Flood the 0s with 4-connectivity: every background pixel reaches the border except (1,1). So H = 1.
Second moment about zero: Σ i² p_i = 0 + 0.25 + 4(0.15) + 9(0.10) = 1.75.

traps: The Euler number is C − H, not C + H. Two pieces with no holes give E = 2, not 0.
Entropy uses log₂ to come out in bits; natural log gives nats and a different number.

Compactness squares the perimeter: P²/A, not P/√A. Dropping the square gives P/√A, and for a circle that is 2√π ≈ 3.54 instead of 12.57. Plain P/A is not dimensionless and changes with the size of the circle, so it is never used.
Variance is the second moment about the mean, not about zero: subtract m² or the answer is far too large.
C and H need mixed connectivity — 8 for the object and 4 for the background, or the reverse. The same rule on both sides breaks the hole count.

quiz.q: Define the Euler number of a binary region.
quiz.a: E = C − H, where C is the number of connected components of the object and H is the number of holes (enclosed background components).

quiz.q: Why is the compactness P²/A a minimum for a circle, and what is that minimum?
quiz.a: A circle encloses the largest area for a given perimeter, so any other shape needs more perimeter for the same area and scores higher. For a circle P²/A = (2πr)² / (πr²) = 4π ≈ 12.57.

quiz.q: A region has area 400 pixels² and perimeter 100 pixels. Find its compactness and say whether it is close to circular.
quiz.a: P²/A = 100² / 400 = 10000 / 400 = 25. The circle value is 12.57, so this region is about twice as 'rough' as a disk — not close to circular.

quiz.q: A two-level region has p₀ = 0.5 and p₁ = 0.5. Find the uniformity and the entropy.
quiz.a: U = 0.5² + 0.5² = 0.5. H_e = −(0.5 log₂ 0.5 + 0.5 log₂ 0.5) = 1 bit, the maximum for two levels.

quiz.q: Two regions have identical area and identical perimeter but look clearly different. Which descriptor separates them, and why does compactness fail?
quiz.a: Compactness is computed from area and perimeter only, so both give the same value. The second moments (eccentricity and principal axis angle) or the skeleton separate them, because those measure how the pixels are distributed inside the outline, not just its length.

quiz.q: In the figure, what goes wrong if 8-connectivity is used for the object and also for the background?
quiz.a: In this figure nothing changes: the hole at (1,1) is a single 0 surrounded by all eight neighbours as 1s, so it touches no other background pixel; H stays 1. The failure appears when the ring has a diagonal step, e.g. 1 1 0 / 1 0 1 / 0 1 1. Then the centre 0 touches the outside 0 at (0,2) diagonally, so with 8-connectivity for the background the hole merges with the outside; H falls to 0 and E becomes 1 instead of 0. Mixed connectivity removes this.

quiz.q: Why does a region with one dominant grey level have high uniformity but low entropy?
quiz.a: Uniformity sums the squares of the probabilities, so a single probability near 1 dominates the sum. Entropy weights each p_i by log₂ p_i, and a probability near 1 contributes almost nothing because log₂ 1 = 0. Concentrating the mass therefore raises U and lowers H_e.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice these descriptors form one feature vector per region, fed to a classifier in Unit 6. Hu's moment invariants make shape numbers rotation- and scale-invariant; only a few universities teach this here. Local binary patterns and HOG replace the global histogram with a per-pixel code and are standard in face and pedestrian detection; see Unit 5. Newer curricula add learned convolutional features, but exams still start from area, compactness, Euler number and co-occurrence contrast.
